extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, art historians, and educated travellers interested in Venetian and Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and prescriptive criteria for identifying, dating, and evaluating Venetian Gothic windows, arches, ornament, materials, and related architectural elements; includes constructional notes and aesthetic principles relevant to Gothic domestic architecture in Venice and nearby mainland cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windows of the second and third orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Second- and third-order windows occur contemporarily; the second story windows of certain Venetian palaces are of the third order, with flanking pilasters and capitals varying constantly in the form of the flower or leaf introduced between their volutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify by paired openings with flanking pilasters and distinctive capital ornament. Use presence of varied leaf/flower ornament between volutes and the pilaster arrangement to classify as second/third order; compare with illustrated typologies (Plate XIV) for precise form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windows of the fourth order
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth order windows first occur in pairs with simple mouldings similar to the second order, later enriching their mouldings (series 4c, 4d, etc.), and are common in many Venetian palaces with great depth of arches and clear detaching of the shafts from the sheets of glass behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize early fourth order as paired simple openings; later conditions show enriched mouldings and bold cusp projection (4d). Note the deep arch profile and that original glazing, when present, would have been set behind the shafts at the same depth. Use depth and shaft detachment as identifying features; compare Venice and Verona variants (4e early Veronese).

rubrics_metrics.name: Windows of the fifth order (mature Gothic arcade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth order windows are a combination of the third and fourth, approximating the 'perfect Gothic' form; arcades of this order are characteristic, with features such as increased size of lateral lights in some groups and cusps ranging from massive (constructive) to perforated (decorative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the union of third- and fourth-order characteristics to identify the fifth order. Observe cusp condition: the more solid the cusp, generally the more ancient; perforated/slender cusps are decorative and occur later. Note that lateral lights are sometimes larger—this is a recurring but unexplained feature. Compare lower bearing traceries (solid cusp) with upper, decorative traceries (perforated cusp) for dating and functional assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trefoiled windows and brick tracery construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Trefoiled windows (among the most ancient Gothic efforts in Venice) are often built entirely of brick except central shaft and capital (Istrian stone); trefoils are cut out of the radiating bricks forming the pointed arch, with roll moulding formed of cast bricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining early trefoiled windows, expect brick-made trefoils, a central stone shaft, pilasters on each side, simple projecting plinths, and square flat brick 'capitals' cast into a primitive cornice form. Their simplicity and the use of cast/moulded bricks indicate early/vernacular workmanship and follow the same compositional 'law of centralization' as grander palaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of centralization in window composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Window groups follow a centralizing scheme: a central shaft, pilasters on each side, then the wall—this 'great law of centralization' is observed even in humble trefoiled windows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate window composition by checking for a clearly emphasized central axis (central shaft) and mirrored side pilasters; this compositional order is a hallmark of Venetian houses following palace systems even at small scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and expressive potential of brick and terra-cotta
rubrics_metrics.description: Brick is a versatile expressive material: adapted from coarse structural bricks to moulded bricks for arches, plinths, and delicate tracery; many Venetian moulded bricks were formed 'in the clay by the hand' so that no two pieces are identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and encourage varied, hand-moulded brick work—use bricks of different sizes, strengths, and hardnesses; employ moulded bricks for decorative tracery and flower-work; treat the brick-field as an 'academy' for learning to handle materials before marble. Judge buildings by how well they exploit brick's possibilities rather than by blind imitation of stone forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional arch forms (reversed curve and condescension to round arch)
rubrics_metrics.description: During transition the pointed arch sometimes adopts a slight reversed curve at its head, making a small concession toward the round arch; such minute concessions indicate transitional forms influenced by mainland examples like Verona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subtle profile changes (reversed curve at arch head) to recognize transitional chronology and cross-regional influences. Compare small Venetian windows showing this concession with mainland arches to trace borrowing and evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or loss of Byzantine ornamentation as a dating indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Venetian Gothic often incorporates Byzantine ornamentation (inlaid alabaster, carved intermediate fields). Later, Byzantine sculpture vanishes leaving marble facing only; this disappearance marks a move toward Gothic simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dating façades, treat residual Byzantine elements (inlaid alabasters, embroidered richness) as evidence of earlier/transitional phases; their absence, with simpler foliage and reduced sculpture, indicates later thirteenth-century Gothic purity. Comparative observation across façades helps place a building in the sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration of the intervals between arches (spandrils and tracery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes experimented included filling spandrils with sculptured emblems (e.g., Evangelists) and occupying wall spaces above windows with intricate quatrefoil tracery. The builder of the Ducal Palace established an arcade model that became the standard for important works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess interval treatment: whether filled by figurative sculpture, quatrefoil tracery, or left as marble facing. Recognize the Ducal Palace arcade arrangement as an influential canonical model for subsequent palaces. Unusual or unique treatments (e.g., Evangelist emblems) are notable exceptions and may be of high documentary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusp condition as a test of age and function
rubrics_metrics.description: The cusp ranges from solid (massive, constructive) to perforated (thin, decorative). Generally, the more solid the cusp, the more ancient it is; perforated cusps are often later and merely decorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cusp mass and penetration as a dating criterion: solid cusps on lower bearing traceries often indicate earlier, structural use; slender, perforated cusps in upper, decorative traceries indicate later decorative developments. Look for stages of thinning leading to perforation to trace chronological sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and detachment of shafts from glazing
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth order examples and some others show great depth of arches and a clear detaching of the shafts from the sheets of glass behind; glass, when anciently used, would have been set behind the shafts at the same depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining windows, note the depth of recess and the relationship of shafts to glazing. A shaft clearly detached from the glazing plane and deep-set glass are indicative of original Gothic practice; modern restorations often alter this relation (e.g., modern balconies or forward-set glazing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and color as primary decorative means (alabaster, serpentine, marbles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some palaces show no sculpture but depend entirely on color and veined stones (e.g., purple alabaster with inlaid green serpentine disks) and on the 'manly simplicity' of capital foliage for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate façades not only by sculpture but by polychromy and material contrast. Color and stone variety can produce magnificent effects without sculptural richness; conservation and attribution should consider original material palettes as integral to design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer pointed arch for structural soundness over square lintel
rubrics_metrics.description: The pointed arch is the best and strongest building form when using ordinary imperfect materials; the common square window with a level brick head is the weakest and often leads to fissures or collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For durable construction in common materials, prefer pointed arches to level lintels. Historical evidence: Veronese brick pointed arches have lasted since the thirteenth century, while many square-headed modern brickwork failures occur within years. The pointed arch both sustains the building above and allows flexible infill of openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional adaptability of Gothic openings for glazing and sashes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no necessity that a pointed arch aperture should have a pointed sash opening; the structural arch may be filled in any convenient way, allowing lancet windows or solid tympana while still accommodating modern sashes and glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or restoring, separate structural arch form from glazing configuration. Fill pointed heads as required—solid slabs, shields, or grouped lights—with thoughtful glazing design (e.g., groups of lancets, gabled canopies) to combine structural virtue with modern convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sculptural narrative programs (e.g., months on archivolts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great central archivolt of St. Mark's displays a sculptural program: figures of the months in sequence, zodiacal signs, and other narrative elements; such sculpture expresses local climate/agricultural customs and Gothic spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret sculptural programs as contextual and symbolic elements: personifications, agricultural labors, and zodiacal symbols can indicate regional practices and the sculptor's intent. When assessing an archivolt, note the sequence, iconography, and any unusual personifications (e.g., Janus forms, local variants) for dating and cultural understanding.
